source_evidence.observation: For a sub-gaussian random variable X, the source asserts both that X - E X is sub-gaussian and that ||X - E X||_{psi_2} <= C ||X||_{psi_2}, where C is an absolute constant.

source_evidence.anchor: Section 2.6.1 opening paragraph immediately before Equation (2.19)
source_evidence.observation: The source defines the operation under discussion as centering X by subtracting its mean and explains that the purpose is to remove a nonzero mean without losing sub-gaussianity.
A random variable is sub-gaussian when it satisfies one of properties (i)-(iv) of Proposition 2.5.2, and its sub-gaussian norm is ||X||_{psi_2} = inf {t > 0 : E exp(X^2/t^2) <= 2}.
The source gives equivalent tail, moment, and exponential-moment characterizations of sub-gaussianity, with their positive parameters comparable by one absolute constant factor.

source_evidence.anchor: Exercise 2.5.7 and the restatement following it, especially Equation (2.15)
source_evidence.observation: The source treats ||.||_{psi_2} as a norm on the space of sub-gaussian random variables and records ||X||_{L^p} <= C ||X||_{psi_2} sqrt(p) for every p >= 1, with C > 0 absolute.

source_evidence.anchor: Proof of Lemma 2.6.8 through Equation (2.20), including footnote 5
source_evidence.observation: The proof invokes the triangle inequality for the psi_2 norm, treats E X as a constant random variable, and defines a ≲ b to mean a <= Cb for some absolute constant C.

source_evidence.anchor: Continuation of the proof of Lemma 2.6.8
source_evidence.observation: The source bounds ||E X||_{psi_2} by an absolute multiple of |E X|, then by E|X| = ||X||_1, and finally by an absolute multiple of ||X||_{psi_2} using Equation (2.15) with p = 1.
The source explicitly asks the reader to show that the centering inequality does not hold with C = 1.

binders: X is an arbitrary scalar random variable to which the sub-gaussian hypothesis is applied. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: Lemma 2.6.8, opening words 'If X is a sub-gaussian random variable'.]

There exists a positive absolute numerical constant C, chosen independently of X and therefore uniform over all such X. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: Lemma 2.6.8, phrase 'where C is an absolute constant'; PDF page 16, printed page 27; anchor: paragraph after Equation (2.16), which writes 'C, c > 0 are absolute constants'.]
hypotheses: X is sub-gaussian. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: Lemma 2.6.8 hypothesis; PDF page 16, printed page 27; anchor: Definition 2.5.6.]
conclusions: The centered random variable X - E X is sub-gaussian. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: Lemma 2.6.8, first conclusion.]
Its sub-gaussian norm satisfies ||X - E X||_{psi_2} <= C ||X||_{psi_2}. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: Lemma 2.6.8, displayed inequality.]
definitions_and_conventions: A random variable Y is sub-gaussian exactly when it satisfies any one of the equivalent properties (i)-(iv) in Proposition 2.5.2. [Source: PDF page 16, printed page 27; anchor: Definition 2.5.6; PDF page 13, printed page 24; anchor: Proposition 2.5.2.]
The psi_2 norm has the exact Orlicz-threshold semantics ||Y||_{psi_2} = inf {t > 0 : E exp(Y^2/t^2) <= 2}. [Source: PDF page 16, printed page 27; anchor: Definition 2.5.6, Equation (2.13).]

The notation ||.||_{psi_2} is used as a genuine norm on the space of sub-gaussian random variables, so in particular the proof uses its triangle inequality. [Source: PDF page 16, printed page 27; anchor: Exercise 2.5.7; PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: proof of Lemma 2.6.8 through Equation (2.20).]
Centering means subtracting the mean: the centered variable is X - E X. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: Section 2.6.1 opening paragraph and Lemma 2.6.8.]

An absolute-constant comparison is a comparison by a numerical constant independent of the random variable; the source's proof convention writes a ≲ b for a <= Cb with C some absolute constant. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: footnote 5 in the proof of Lemma 2.6.8.]
implicit_context: The expectation E X is finite for sub-gaussian X: Equation (2.15) at p = 1 bounds ||X||_1 by an absolute multiple of ||X||_{psi_2}, and the proof of Lemma 2.6.8 uses exactly this specialization. [Source: PDF page 16, printed page 27; anchor: Equation (2.15); PDF page 20, printed page 31; anchor: proof continuation ending 'using (2.15) with p = 1'.]

When ||E X||_{psi_2} occurs, E X is regarded as the constant random variable with that value. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: proof sentence 'for any constant random variable a' and the substitution a = E X; PDF page 20, printed page 31; anchor: first line of the proof continuation.]

The same psi_2 norm defined by Equation (2.13) is used on both X and X - E X. [Source: PDF page 16, printed page 27; anchor: Definition 2.5.6 and Equation (2.13); PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: Lemma 2.6.8 displayed inequality.]

details: One absolute constant C > 0 works uniformly for every sub-gaussian random variable X; C is not allowed to depend on X or its distribution. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: Lemma 2.6.8, phrase 'where C is an absolute constant', together with footnote 5's absolute-constant convention; PDF page 16, printed page 27; anchor: 'C, c > 0 are absolute constants'.]

The sole stated hypothesis is sub-gaussianity of X; the lemma does not assume that X is already mean zero or that X is independent of another random variable. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: complete statement of Lemma 2.6.8 and the Section 2.6.1 motivation concerning variables that do not have zero means.]
The contract contains both preservation of sub-gaussianity under centering and the quantitative psi_2-norm estimate. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: complete statement of Lemma 2.6.8.]

The threshold in the defining exponential-moment condition is exactly 2, the scale variable satisfies t > 0, and the norm is the infimum of all admissible scales. [Source: PDF page 16, printed page 27; anchor: Definition 2.5.6, Equation (2.13).]

The definition applies to the full random variable and uses E exp(Y^2/t^2), not a centered moment, variance, tail proxy, or MGF of Y. [Source: PDF page 16, printed page 27; anchor: Definition 2.5.6, Equation (2.13).]

The lemma claims only an unspecified absolute constant and does not claim the sharp factor 1; the following exercise states that C = 1 does not work in general. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: Lemma 2.6.8 and footnote 5; PDF page 20, printed page 31; anchor: Exercise 2.6.9.]

undebatable_constraints: The quantification must permit a single positive absolute C that is independent of X and works for all sub-gaussian X. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: Lemma 2.6.8, phrase 'where C is an absolute constant', and footnote 5; PDF page 16, printed page 27; anchor: 'C, c > 0 are absolute constants'.]

The only input condition is that X is sub-gaussian; no mean-zero, symmetry, boundedness, or independence condition may be added. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: complete hypothesis of Lemma 2.6.8.]

The centered object must be X - E X, not X minus a median, an arbitrary constant, or an independent copy. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: Section 2.6.1 opening paragraph and Lemma 2.6.8.]
Both conclusions are required: X - E X is sub-gaussian and ||X - E X||_{psi_2} <= C ||X||_{psi_2}. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: complete conclusion of Lemma 2.6.8.]
Every occurrence of the psi_2 norm must have the Equation (2.13) semantics inf {t > 0 : E exp(Y^2/t^2) <= 2}. [Source: PDF page 16, printed page 27; anchor: Definition 2.5.6, Equation (2.13).]
The right-hand side is the psi_2 norm of the original uncentered X, multiplied only by the absolute constant C. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: displayed inequality in Lemma 2.6.8.]
The constant must not be fixed to 1, because the source explicitly says the inequality fails with C = 1 in general. [Source: PDF page 20, printed page 31; anchor: Exercise 2.6.9.]

ambiguities.issue: The source does not specify a numerical value or an optimal value for C.
ambiguities.evidence: Lemma 2.6.8 calls C merely 'an absolute constant', and its proof uses the suppressed-comparison notation ≲; Exercise 2.6.9 only rules out C = 1. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: Lemma statement, proof, and footnote 5; PDF page 20, printed page 31; anchor: Exercise 2.6.9.]
ambiguities.impact: A faithful contract may existentially quantify an unspecified positive universal constant, but it may not attribute a particular numerical or sharp constant to the source. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: phrase 'where C is an absolute constant' and footnote 5; PDF page 20, printed page 31; anchor: Exercise 2.6.9.]

contracts.contract_plain_english: There is one positive numerical constant C, independent of the choice and distribution of X, such that every sub-gaussian random variable X remains sub-gaussian after subtracting its mean and satisfies ||X - E X||_{psi_2} <= C ||X||_{psi_2}. Here ||Y||_{psi_2} means exactly inf {t > 0 : E exp(Y^2/t^2) <= 2}; the source leaves C unspecified and explicitly notes that C = 1 is not valid in general. [Source: PDF page 19, printed page 30; anchor: Lemma 2.6.8, its displayed inequality, proof through Equation (2.20), and footnote 5; PDF page 16, printed page 27; anchor: Definition 2.5.6 and Equation (2.13); PDF page 20, printed page 31; anchor: proof conclusion and Exercise 2.6.9.]
